1 · Introduction

Observation: I reviewed the pipeline workflow video and observed the importance of establishing a standardized project folder hierarchy and living documentation before writing any code or importing random assets. Useful Idea & Interpretation: A core idea is that a solid, predetermined folder structure combined with modular ReadMe/HTML files isn't just file management—it is a team communication tool. When every team member knows exactly where models, scripts, audio, and documentation belong, onboarding is seamless and the risk of merge conflicts or misplaced dependencies is greatly reduced. Question: What naming conventions and folder templates does our team plan to agree upon so we avoid broken references when sharing assets in Unity/version control?

2 · Developer mindset

Observation: I reviewed the developer mindset video and observed that technical setbacks and bugs are framed not as personal shortcomings, but as normal, necessary milestones in the development cycle. Useful Idea & Interpretation: A core idea presented is treating failure as data rather than defeat. In software and game development, builds break and features fail routinely. Having a growth mindset means actively dissecting mistakes, embracing challenges outside our current comfort zone, and focusing on effort rather than fixed ability so that roadblocks turn into learning opportunities. Question: When we run into code or design failures during sprints, what process will we use as a team to debrief and troubleshoot without placing blame?

3 · Folders and project creation

Observation: I reviewed the folder and project setup demonstration and observed how establishing a dedicated directory structure (such as separating Context, Requirements, Resources, and dedicated game build folders) prevents clutter before any engine work begins. Useful Idea & Interpretation: A critical idea is structuring folders not just for personal convenience, but for team accessibility and onboarding. By utilizing JSON templates or standardized folder blueprints that include local ReadMe files and requirement checklists, any new team member can immediately understand where assets live, what each folder is for, and what prerequisites are needed without constant back-and-forth communication. Question: What core folder structure and root path naming rules will our team enforce before creating the shared Unity repository to ensure everyone stays consistent?

4 · Documentation

Observation: I reviewed the documentation video and observed that a Game Development Document (GDD) is treated not as a static, one-time chore, but as a living blueprint that evolves alongside the game as mechanics and milestones are tested. Useful Idea & Interpretation: A central idea is that documentation acts as the single source of truth for the entire team—defining the narrative, core game loop, required art/audio assets, and individual member responsibilities. My interpretation is that having clear, centralized documentation prevents disputes and scope creep because every decision is measured against the agreed-upon design pillars rather than vague assumptions. Question: Who on our team will be responsible for keeping the GDD updated as we iterate, and where will it be hosted so everyone has real-time access?

5 · Introduction to Unity

Observation: I reviewed the introduction to Unity video and observed the core layout of the Unity Editor—specifically the relationship between the Hierarchy (objects currently in the scene), Scene view (3D editor viewport), Game view (rendered player camera), Inspector (object properties and components), and the Project window (asset file structure). Useful Idea & Interpretation: Mastering viewport navigation shortcuts (holding Alt + Left Click to orbit, Middle Click to pan, and pressing F to focus/frame a selected object) along with Ctrl + D to duplicate assets is essential for developer velocity. Being comfortable navigating 3D space and quickly switching between Scene and Game view prevents disorientation and allows team members to build and iterate on environments much faster. Question: What default editor layout and common tool settings should our team standardize so our screens and workflows look consistent during screen shares or pairing sessions?

6 · Import a custom player

Observation: I reviewed the custom player import video and observed how a 3D model (like an FBX downloaded from Mixamo) can immediately inherit existing controller logic and animations by setting its Rig Animation Type to Humanoid and assigning its new Avatar to the player's Animator component. Useful Idea & Interpretation: Unity’s Humanoid rig system acts as a universal bone-mapping bridge. As long as our imported custom character and the template controller are both rigged as Humanoid avatars, we don't have to rebuild running, jumping, or sprint animations from scratch. This allows our art team to swap character models effortlessly while keeping core gameplay mechanics intact. Question: What character scale and bone naming conventions will our artists follow in Mixamo/Blender to ensure custom models retarget cleanly to Unity’s Humanoid avatar system?

My interpretation

Observation: Connecting our pipeline videos to my concept for StimuLye (where the protagonist "NaN" reconstructs a hospital and liminal memory rooms from total darkness), I decided that our team must strictly limit our initial build to the "Vertical Slice" demonstrated in the pipeline—focusing only on the dark opening, one looping ward corridor, and one interactive memory room. Useful Idea & Interpretation: The pipeline's emphasis on modular Prefabs and scope management is the exact vehicle needed to make StimuLye playable. In the story, interacting with "Stimuli" objects restores stability to the dark void. By building our hospital walls, doors, and memory props as modular Unity prefabs with shared materials, we can dynamically spawn or trigger room transformations without having to hand-model endless unique rooms. Furthermore, formalizing this in our GDD keeps us from expanding into all four acts before the core sensory-restoration mechanic actually feels compelling. Question: How can we design our modular corridor and room prefabs so that a simple material or lighting swap can visually transition the hospital from normal to decaying liminal space as "Static" approaches?

02 · My contribution

My understanding of the job

What I Did / Decided / Observed: Moving from the preparation phase into active contribution, I observed that our objective is not to jump blindly into coding a full game, but to execute a standardized development pipeline. I decided that our team's immediate mission must focus on delivering a cohesive, playable vertical slice rather than getting bogged down in feature bloat. The Work (What Needs to Be Done): "The work" means setting up a structured foundation before building out content. This involves: Establishing a clean, shallow directory structure (/Context, /Requirements, /Resources, /Assets/StimuLye/) and initializing our living GDD with clear Lead/Support role assignments. Setting up the Unity project with a verified Third-Person template to secure immediate movement physics and camera controls. Importing and retargeting our custom 3D model (swapping the default mannequin with NaN’s avatar via Unity's Humanoid rig system). Building modular corridor and room prefabs to establish the environment. The Finish Line (Definition of Done): The finish line is not a finished four-act game; it is a playable Vertical Slice prototype (MVP). Completion means having a stable, testable build where a player wakes up in the dark, navigates the opening ward corridor, and successfully interacts with a "Stimuli" item that visibly stabilizes a memory room without errors or broken dependencies. Question / Next Step: Once we verify that the player can walk through the corridor and trigger the first room transition, what specific performance and gameplay metrics will we test during our huddle?

Production pipeline

Unnamed stage Unnamed stage I used mermaid · owner Lexxie Mermaid worked better for me. Production Pipeline Explanation: StimuLye Vertical Slice (AAA Framework) Our production pipeline applies Dr. Malik Stalbert's AAA Framework (Application → Action → Amplification) to transition our team smoothly from an initial template into a playable, narrative-driven prototype: 1. Stage 1: Application (Setup & Baseline) Following the principle that "application gets them moving," we do not start by writing code from scratch. We establish our shallow directory structure (D:\PROJECTS\StimuLye) to bypass Windows path length limits and deploy Unity's verified Third Person Core template. This gives us immediate physics, camera orbit, and movement controls within 30 minutes. 2. Stages 2 & 3: Action (Mechanics, Avatars & Environments) Once the baseline is alive, the team enters the "Action" phase, where concepts and custom assets are introduced: - Character Integration: We import our NaN model, set its rig to Humanoid, safely unpack the player armature, and swap the geometry. The Humanoid avatar acts as the bridge so existing template animations retarget cleanly to our custom protagonist. - Environment Construction: Our level designer uses modular prefabs (the "cookie-cutter" approach) to build the looping hospital ward and dark memory rooms without wasting memory. 3. Stage 4 & 5: Amplification (Core Loop, Polish & Verification) In the "Amplification" phase, private technical competence expands into an integrated experience: - Core Narrative Mechanic: We implement the "Stimuli" interaction script. Picking up the sensory object triggers a room material swap from dark void to stable hospital textures while playing the first "Static" audio cue. - Verification & Team Review: The team conducts an end-to-end playtest, verifying that the opening dark sequence, corridor movement, and memory stabilization run smoothly with zero console errors. Roles & Time Estimates: - Block 1 (30m): Technical Lead (Template & Directories) - Block 2 (45m): 3D Artist / Character Lead (Rigging & Retargeting) - Block 3 (60m): Level Designer (Modular Ward Prefabs) - Block 4 (60m): Gameplay Programmer & Audio Lead (Stimuli Triggers) - Block 5 (45m): QA & Entire Team (Playtest & Milestone Sign-off) Total Sprint Duration: 4 Hours (240 Minutes)

Engine, assets + technology

What I Did / Decided / Observed: As a solo developer on StimuLye, my priority is eliminating pipeline friction so I don't get overwhelmed wearing every hat alone. I applied the TnT ("Tool and the Temple") principle: every tool must serve my MVP vertical slice and reduce manual labor. I chose a lean, verified stack built on Unity 6.6 and established personal testing gates to check my own work at each milestone. My Agreed Solo Tool Stack & Verification Plan: Engine: Unity 6.6 (6000.6) with URP Why: Faster Play Mode entry, lighter memory footprint, and native Universal Render Pipeline lighting/fog to achieve StimuLye’s dark atmosphere without third-party render plugins. Who Checks It: Me (wearing the Technical Hat) — verified via build tests and frame rate checks. Language & IDE: C# / Visual Studio Community Why: Standard Unity scripting for clean, fast implementation of the "Stimuli" interaction and room material swap trigger scripts. Who Checks It: Me (wearing the Programmer Hat) — verified with zero console errors and clean syntax. Base Template: Starter Assets – Third Person Controller + Cinemachine Why: Provides an instant movement, sprint, jump, and camera follow baseline. As a solo dev, this saves me dozens of hours of physics and camera programming so I can focus directly on the story mechanics. Who Checks It: Me (wearing the Technical Hat) — verified through Play Mode controller feel. Art & Rigging: Mixamo + Blender Why: Mixamo automatically generates the Humanoid rig and Avatar for my custom "NaN" character; Blender is used for quick adjustments and whiteboxing modular ward prefabs. Who Checks It: Me (wearing the Visual Hat) — verified by checking that animations retarget without bone stretching. Audio: Audacity / FreeSound (WAV stems) Why: Simple, lightweight sound editing for hospital room tone, heart monitor beeps, and the "Static" cue. Who Checks It: Me (wearing the Audio Hat) — verified with in-engine volume balance checks. Progress Tracking: Git + Project_LOG.txt Why: Local Git commits protect my project from corruption; the auto-timestamped .LOG file holds me accountable to daily tasks. Who Checks It: Me (wearing the QA / Architect Hat) — audited against my GDD checklist. Question / Self-Check: How can I automate my daily .LOG entries and Git commits so project tracking remains effortless while working solo?

Future reuse + credits

What I Did / Decided / Observed: Thinking beyond this initial prototype assignment, I audited our production assets to determine what foundational systems can be reused across Act 2 (The Ward), Act 3 (The Deep), and the Finale without rebuilding from scratch. I decided to maintain a strict licensing and attribution log in /Requirements/ so all third-party credit requirements are tracked before scaling the game. Reusable Components, Sources & Credit Requirements: Core Character Controller & Camera Rig: What is Reusable: The PlayerArmature with Third-Person movement physics, jump/sprint logic, and Cinemachine orbital follow camera. Source: Unity Technologies (Starter Assets – Third Person Character Controller). Credit / License: Unity Companion License / Asset Store Terms. Free for commercial and non-commercial compiled builds; requires standard Unity engine inclusion in game credits. Protagonist Model & Rigging: What is Reusable: The Humanoid bone hierarchy, animation controller mapping, and custom "NaN" mesh. Source: Adobe Mixamo (Erika_Archer base mesh & standard Humanoid locomotion clips). Credit / License: Royalty-free under Adobe Mixamo Terms of Service for use in embedded video game builds (attribution to Adobe Mixamo in credits; raw .fbx files cannot be redistributed open-source). Modular Room & Corridor Prefab Kit: What is Reusable: Floor, wall, and doorway prefabs that can be re-skinned into decaying Backrooms/liminal spaces for Act 3 using shader/material swaps. Source: Custom-modeled in Blender / Unity primitives. Credit / License: Original creator IP — 100% owned, no third-party attribution required. "Stimuli" Trigger & Room Stabilization Scripts: What is Reusable: The event-driven C# interaction architecture (StimulusItem.cs, RoomStabilizer.cs) can power every memory puzzle across all remaining chapters. Source: Custom original C# codebase. Credit / License: Original creator IP — fully reusable across future episodes or spinoff projects. Audio & Distortion Cues: What is Reusable: Heartbeat pulses, hospital ambient drone, and the "Static" entity audio stems. Source: Pixabay / FreeSound.org. Credit / License: Pixabay Content License / Creative Commons (CC-BY 4.0 / CC0). Requires listing contributing sound artist handles in the game's final end-credits roll. Question / Next Step: Should I set up an automated Credits.txt file inside /Requirements/ now so that attribution for new sound stems and models is recorded the moment they are downloaded?

04 · Execute + return

Return-to-work review

☑ Goal understood · ☑ Owners and deadlines confirmed · ☑ Blockers and checks reviewed

What I understand: My goal is a beautiful, playable scene in Unity with a 3D player seen in third person. My plan is to build one small vertical slice of StimuLye, not the whole game. The slice is a dark opening, one looping ward corridor, and one Stimuli memory room that changes when the player picks up an item. I'll use Unity 6.6 with URP and the Third Person Starter Assets, so movement and the camera work from the start. The plan has five stages: Setup, NaN avatar, ward prefabs, the Stimuli mechanic, and a playtest. I test after every stage and keep a Project_LOG.txt, so I can see what changed if something breaks. My job: I'm working solo, so I do every role. As technical lead I set up the project and Git. As the 3D artist I import and rig the NaN character from Mixamo. As the level designer I build the modular ward prefabs. As the programmer I write StimulusItem and RoomStabilizer. As QA I playtest for errors and frame rate. I also keep a credits file for every outside asset I use. What I need to clarify: (1) Is the vertical slice small enough for me to finish and test alone? (2) Does "beautiful" mean polished lighting, fog and materials, or is a clean whitebox with good atmosphere enough? (3) Do I need a specific Unity version or template for this assignment, and will it still work if Unity updates packages mid-project? (4) Which free assets and audio am I allowed to use, and how should I credit them? I'm ready to move on to the whiteboard.

Solo review, so I checked each statement myself. Goal and finish line: I'm aiming for a beautiful, playable Unity scene with a 3D third-person player. My finish line is one working vertical slice (dark opening, looping ward corridor, one Stimuli memory room) that plays with no console errors. Next task, deadline and dependencies: My next task is stage 1, setting up the Unity 6.6 project with the Third Person Starter Assets and Project_LOG.txt. Each later stage depends on the one before it: avatar, then ward prefabs, then the Stimuli scripts, then the playtest. I can't start the Stimuli scripts until the avatar and prefabs both work. I'll finish one stage per work session and keep one Git commit per stage. Blockers and how I'll check results: The main blocker is a Unity 6.6 package update breaking the Starter Assets, which Git rollbacks cover. I'll check each stage by running it in Play mode (WASD, jump, camera, no pink shaders, no clipping), and the final check is 0 errors and a stable 60 FPS. What changed: I narrowed the scope from the full game to one slice, and every outside asset now gets credited in Credits.txt. Needs attention: I still need to confirm how detailed "beautiful" needs to be (lighting and materials versus a clean whitebox) and which assets I'm allowed to use.

Failure -> fix -> retest (Git push): When I pushed my reorganized folder, GitHub rejected it with error GH001 because a 209 MB file, Week12/12B.zip, was in my commit and GitHub's limit is 100 MB. That zip was only a transfer copy and should never have been committed. Deleting the file in a later commit did not help, because the zip was still in the unpushed history. Fix: I ran git reset --soft origin/main to undo my two unpushed commits while keeping my files, removed the zip from Git and from disk, added *.zip to .gitignore, and checked with git status that no file over 100 MB was staged. Retest: I committed again and the push succeeded. The largest remaining files are two template lightmaps (about 27 MB and 23 MB), which are under the limit. Lesson: check git status for large files before committing. Other issue noted: my earlier planning notes say URP, but the project uses HDRP. I documented this in README.md section 9.

Result compared with the mission

Mission: Make a beautiful playable scene in Unity with a 3D player viewed in third person, built as a StimuLye vertical slice (dark opening, looping ward corridor, one Stimuli memory room). What I verified (observed): The Unity 6.6 (6000.6.7f1) High Definition 3D template opens and runs in Play mode. The third-person player is already in the scene and controllable (WASD, Shift, Space), and the Console showed 0 errors and 1 warning (HDRP "ScriptableRuntimeReflectionSystemSettings.system is assigned more than once", from the template). Evidence: Evidence/testfixconsole.png. I also organized the repo (Context, Requirements, Resources, Evidence, project-source), wrote a README with all paths and reproduction steps, and pushed it to GitHub after fixing a push rejection caused by a 209 MB zip that I had committed by mistake. Useful discovery: The template already provides the third-person player, camera and a high-quality lit scene, so the "beautiful scene + third-person player" part of my goal works before I build anything custom. This changes my plan: instead of spending time on a controller, I should spend it on the StimuLye content. I also discovered that my planning notes assumed URP, but the template is HDRP, which is heavier and means my C# package table (UnityEngine.Rendering.Universal) is wrong for this project. Finally, I learned to check git status for large files before committing, because GitHub rejects files over 100 MB. What remains (not yet done or tested): importing the NaN model (Mixamo, Humanoid rig) into PlayerArmature; building modular ward and corridor prefabs in Assets/StimuLye/Prefabs; writing StimulusItem and RoomStabilizer in Assets/StimuLye/Scripts; adding the Static audio cue; and measuring frame rate and console errors in a final playtest. The Assets/StimuLye folders exist but are empty. Next steps: (1) decide whether to keep HDRP or switch to URP, and update the documentation to match, (2) import NaN and test the swap, which is where I expect my first failure, fix and retest, (3) whitebox one corridor and one memory room with prefabs, (4) write the Stimulus scripts and test that pickup changes the room, (5) playtest for 0 errors and stable FPS and record the result in Project_LOG.txt. Unresolved question: Is HDRP acceptable for this assignment, or should I use URP as I planned? I will keep HDRP unless told otherwise, because the template already works.
